entities.name: Emperor An of Han
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Emperor An of Han (Liu Hu), the sixth ruler of the Eastern Han dynasty, reigned from 106 to 125 CE, presiding over a pivotal period of accelerating imperial decline. Ascending the throne at the tender age of twelve as the grandson of Emperor Zhang, his reign became a stark illustration of the escalating power struggles between imperial consort clans and eunuch factions, fundamentally eroding the central authority that had defined the dynasty's earlier strength. His rule is critical for understanding the institutional weaknesses that ultimately precipitated the Eastern Han's fragmentation.

An's early years were dominated by the regency of Empress Dowager Deng Sui, a capable but firm ruler who maintained relative stability but effectively sidelined the young emperor. Upon Deng Sui's death in 121 CE, An, now an adult, swiftly purged the Deng clan, consolidating power by elevating his wet nurse Wang Sheng and influential eunuchs such as Jiang Jing and Li Run. This shift unleashed an era of widespread corruption and arbitrary rule, characterized by frequent dismissals and executions of provincial officials, often on fabricated charges, as these favored cliques amassed immense wealth and influence. Concurrently, costly and largely inconclusive military campaigns against the Qiang people in the western provinces further strained the imperial treasury.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Emperor An's reign is a critical case study in the decline of the Eastern Han, as his empowerment of eunuchs and consort families directly led to a century of intense factionalism and weakened imperial authority. This systemic instability contributed significantly to the eventual fragmentation of the Han empire into the Three Kingdoms period.
